source_text:
Show HN: PanelAlpha Engine – Turn your VPS into a programmable hosting layer
PanelAlpha Engine is an open-source hosting environment for your VPS, programmable through MCP, API and CLI. After ~2 years in the making (we started back in the non-ai era) we've decided to open source our Docker-based Engine. So far, we've used it as a back-end environment for WordPress sites and we have been distributing it through web hosting providers and larger agencies. It's been tested on a few thousand sites already. Now people are vibe coding, using AI for everything and building agentic workflows, while at the same time open source projects are getting through a reinassaince. So, not only we have open-sourced it ourselves, but we've also expanded it to support any web application and tested it against over a thousand repositories (and soon will be much more). You can use it with MCP, API or CLI to:
- deploy projects from files or git
- get a preview URL or use your own domain with automatic SSL
- restrict access with a password
- get built-in monitoring and visitor stats (no need for Google Analytics)
- manage databases, SFTP/FTP, CRON, firewall rules
- read through logs and debug
- create or restore backups (locally or remotely via S3/FTP)
- connect with Cloudflare (for tunnels and DNS)
... and much more (see docs). You install it with one command (you can also define a repo to be installed together with it) and then with another command connect your AI with it. Done. Your agent gets a hosting environment on your server without unrestricted root SSH access. You can even define its permissions. Our early users have asked us about the visual/panel - it will be available soon too (and also open source). Feel free to roast, we're open for feedback!

## Goal
Populate correctly matched, rights-cleared, real packaging photos for **all 45** current master catalogue entries, starting with the **22 configured products**. Do not mark completed until every currently stocked drink displays its actual package photo during sale selection.

Public-read only for nonsensitive product packaging. Upload and delete owner-only; 1 MB JPEG/PNG/WebP bucket limit. Do not change stock, prices, crate obligations, or customer data.

> Not sure what to tell you. It's been a problem for decades and only gets worse It's been a problem for literally millennia. This hardly unique to 21
> Not sure what to tell you. It's been a problem for decades and only gets worse It's been a problem for literally millennia. This hardly unique to 21st century america. Yes, I'm glad you don't have a "problem child". That's genuinely great, I wish everyone was that lucky. What I would  like , in the smallest possible way, is some shred of empathy for people who aren't as lucky as you are. Perhaps you could practice the concept of "walking a mile in another man's shoes" and make an attempt to understand what they're dealing with instead of dismissing them as inferior. I'm also happy your wife is volunteering to help with girl scouts. I think that's a great thing and more people should do it. But that doesn't excuse your lack of empathy. Kids are not some kind of deterministic automatons where the same input always produces the same output (as if we could even reproduce the same inputs for an entire life). They're more complicated than that for reasons we frankly can't even understand. There are a number of things that are highly correlated with producing a "good child", a major one being having enough money that the family isn't under constant stress and you can afford second (or third or fourth) chances. But callously discarding every child who isn't lucky enough to benefit from this is just wrong. We, as a society, a culture, should be better than that. Am I expecting you, personally, to go out and change the world? No, no more than I'm expecting myself to do it. But we all make small decisions every day and if enough of us make the "right ones" they can add up, and it starts with empathy for our fellow man.

GMP Certification in Indonesia
GMP Certification in Indonesia – Good Manufacturing Practices
GMP Certification in Indonesia helps manufacturers establish controlled, hygienic, and consistent production practices that support product quality and safety. GMP, or Good Manufacturing Practices, provides principles for controlling manufacturing activities so products are produced and handled according to defined quality requirements.
GMP is particularly relevant to industries such as pharmaceuticals, food and beverages, cosmetics, medical devices, dietary supplements, and other sectors where manufacturing conditions can directly affect product safety and quality. Organizations can use GMP principles to strengthen production controls, documentation, hygiene, quality assurance, and traceability.
For professional guidance, explore[ GMP Certification in Indonesia](https://certvalue.com/gmp-certification-in-indonesia/).
What Is GMP Certification in Indonesia?
GMP Certification in Indonesia generally refers to an assessment, certification, inspection, or compliance process against applicable Good Manufacturing Practice requirements. The exact requirements depend on the product category, industry, applicable regulations, and relevant regulatory or certification scheme.
GMP focuses on controlling manufacturing risks throughout the product lifecycle. It can cover raw materials, personnel, facilities, equipment, production processes, quality control, sanitation, packaging, storage, documentation, and distribution.
Indonesian manufacturers may need to consider requirements established by relevant authorities, including the Indonesian Food and Drug Authority (BPOM), together with sector-specific regulations and customer requirements. Organizations should determine which GMP requirements and regulatory approvals apply to their specific products.
Why Is GMP Important for Indonesian Businesses?
Indonesia's manufacturing sector supplies products to both domestic and international markets. Maintaining consistent production conditions is essential for organizations whose products can affect consumer health, safety, or product performance.
GMP provides a systematic approach to identifying and controlling manufacturing risks. It encourages organizations to maintain suitable facilities, control raw materials, train employees, monitor processes, maintain equipment, and keep accurate production records.
Effective GMP practices can also support preparation for regulatory inspections, customer audits, supplier evaluations, and applicable market requirements. However, GMP certification or assessment does not automatically replace product registrations, licenses, approvals, or other legally required authorizations.
Benefits of GMP Certification in Indonesia
1. Consistent Product Quality
GMP controls help organizations standardize manufacturing activities and reduce variations that could affect product quality.
2. Improved Product Safety
Hygiene controls, sanitation procedures, equipment maintenance, and process monitoring can help reduce contamination and manufacturing-related risks.
3. Better Regulatory Preparedness
A structured GMP system can help organizations organize manufacturing activities around applicable regulatory and industry requirements.
4. Stronger Documentation and Traceability
Accurate production records, batch information, inspection results, and corrective action records help organizations track manufacturing activities and investigate quality issues.
5. Increased Customer Confidence
Documented manufacturing controls can provide customers, distributors, and business partners with greater confidence in an organization's production practices.
6. Reduced Operational Risks
Employee training, preventive maintenance, process controls, and defined procedures can reduce production errors, contamination risks, and inconsistent outputs.
Key Elements of GMP in Indonesia
An effective GMP framework commonly addresses:
Personnel: Appropriate training, hygiene, responsibilities, and competency.
Facilities: Suitable premises designed and maintained to support hygienic operations.
Equipment: Properly selected, cleaned, maintained, and controlled equipment.
Raw Materials: Controlled sourcing, inspection, identification, storage, and handling.
Production: Approved procedures and controlled manufacturing processes.
Quality Control: Appropriate inspection, testing, and product evaluation.
Documentation: Accurate procedures, production records, inspection records, and corrective actions.
Storage and Distribution: Controlled conditions that help preserve product quality.
GMP Certification Process in Indonesia
The process varies according to the industry, product, applicable regulations, and assessment arrangement.
Step 1: Initial Review
The organization identifies its products, manufacturing activities, applicable GMP requirements, and regulatory obligations.
Step 2: Gap Assessment
Facilities, processes, documentation, hygiene practices, equipment, and quality controls are reviewed to identify gaps.
Step 3: GMP System Development
Required procedures for production, sanitation, quality control, maintenance, training, documentation, and other activities are established or improved.
Step 4: Implementation and Training
Employees implement approved procedures and maintain appropriate records throughout manufacturing operations.
Step 5: Internal Evaluation
Internal audits, inspections, or management reviews may be conducted to identify weaknesses and corrective actions.
Step 6: Assessment and Corrective Action
The applicable inspection, assessment, certification, or regulatory process is completed and identified issues are addressed.
Step 7: Final Documentation
Certification, inspection records, regulatory documentation, or other evidence is issued according to the applicable scheme.
Why Choose CertValue for GMP Support in Indonesia?
CertValue provides consulting and certification-related support for organizations seeking to improve their manufacturing and compliance practices. Indonesian businesses can obtain guidance on GMP requirements, documentation, procedures, implementation, internal reviews, and assessment preparation.
The appropriate assessment depends on the product category, industry, applicable regulations, and selected certification or regulatory arrangement. Organizations should confirm whether they require certification, regulatory approval, inspection, registration, or another form of conformity documentation.
For more information, visit[ GMP Certification in Indonesia](https://certvalue.com/gmp-certification-in-indonesia/).
Conclusion
GMP Certification in Indonesia helps organizations establish controlled manufacturing practices focused on product quality, safety, consistency, hygiene, and traceability. By implementing appropriate procedures and maintaining effective production controls, businesses can strengthen their manufacturing operations and improve readiness for applicable regulatory and customer requirements.
Organizations seeking GMP implementation and certification-related support can contact CertValue for guidance on applicable requirements and available services.

Help Needed: Building an AI-Powered Personalized Fitness Plan Automation with n8n + Google Forms + WhatsApp
Hi everyone, 
 I’m currently working on an  AI-powered fitness automation using n8n , and I would appreciate some guidance from the community on how to design the workflow properly. 
 The basic idea is to create an automated system where a user first fills out a  Google Form  with their personal fitness requirements. The form would collect information such as: 
 
 
 Name 
 
 
 Age 
 
 
 Current weight 
 
 
 Target weight 
 
 
 Fitness goal 
 
 
 General fitness 
 
 
 Weight loss 
 
 
 Weight gain 
 
 
 Muscle building 
 
 
 Other goals 
 
 
 
 
 Current fitness level 
 
 
 Type of workout they prefer 
 
 
 Gym 
 
 
 Home workout 
 
 
 Outdoor workout 
 
 
 
 
 Available workout time 
 
 
 Dietary preferences 
 
 
 Food preferences/restrictions 
 
 
 Number of meals they prefer 
 
 
 Any relevant limitations or conditions they want the system to consider 
 
 
   Proposed n8n Workflow 
 I’m thinking of building something like: 
  Google Form → Google Sheets → n8n → AI → Personalized Fitness Plan → WhatsApp  
 After the user submits the form, n8n would collect and process the information and send it to an AI model. 
 The AI would then generate a  personalized daily fitness plan , including: 
    Workout Plan  
 
 
 Exercises for the day 
 
 
 Sets and repetitions 
 
 
 Workout duration 
 
 
 Rest periods 
 
 
 Gym/home workout variations 
 
 
    Daily Meal Plan  
 
 
 Breakfast 
 
 
 Lunch 
 
 
 Snacks 
 
 
 Dinner 
 
 
 Suggested food options 
 
 
 Approximate calorie and protein targets 
 
 
    Daily Targets  
 
 
 Estimated calorie target 
 
 
 Protein target 
 
 
 Water intake 
 
 
 Daily activity/step goal 
 
 
 Workout duration 
 
 
    Personalized Schedule  
The system should ideally generate a plan based on the user’s goal and preferences and provide a different daily plan as the user progresses. 
   WhatsApp Automation 
 Once the plan is generated, I want n8n to automatically send it to the user through  WhatsApp . 
 For example: 
 
  Good Morning, Rahul!    
   Goal: Weight Loss 
  Today’s Target: ~2,000 kcal 
  Water: 2.5–3 L 
    Today’s Workout  
• Squats – 3 × 12 
• Push-ups – 3 × 10 
• Walking – 30 min 
    Breakfast  
• Eggs + oats + fruit 
    Lunch  
• Rice/roti + vegetables + protein source 
    Dinner  
• … 
 Have a great workout!   
 
 I would also like to eventually add  daily reminders , progress tracking, and possibly allow users to update their weight or progress through WhatsApp. 
   What I Need Help With 
 I would especially appreciate suggestions on: 
 
 
  How should I structure the n8n workflow?  
 
 
 Which nodes would be best for processing the Google Form/Google Sheets data? 
 
 
 What is the best way to structure the  AI prompt  so that the generated plans are consistent and personalized? 
 
 
 How should I maintain a user’s information and progress over multiple days? 
 
 
 What is the best approach for sending the generated plan through  WhatsApp ? 
 
 
 How can I create a system where the AI generates a new plan each day rather than repeating the same plan? 
 
 
 What would be the best database/storage option for user profiles and progress? 
 
 
 Are there any important things I should consider regarding  fitness, nutrition, calorie calculations, and user safety ? 
 
 
 I’m fairly new to building larger n8n workflows, so I would really appreciate  a recommended architecture or example workflow  that I can use as a starting point. 
 Thanks in advance!   
I’d love to hear suggestions from anyone who has built similar  AI + n8n + WhatsApp automation systems .

source_text:
I think a lot of us are trying really hard here to avoid the simplest and most obvious answer, which is that AI coding software is helpful, but doesn'
I think a lot of us are trying really hard here to avoid the simplest and most obvious answer, which is that AI coding software is helpful, but doesn't deliver the kind of productivity gains boosters are talking about. There's a bunch of reasons for this, but the obvious one to me is just that I haven't seen  any  backed up claims that actually break down how a 10x (or similar) speed up would get delivered in practice. For the sake of an example, let's imagine an engineer who works an 8 hour day split up like this: - 2 hours: investigating and debugging potential issues - 1 hour: reviewing code - 2 hours: in various team meetings, catch ups or otherwise - 1 hour: designing (including at a level of writing code for prototyping etc) - 2 hours: actually writing code I think that's a semi-reasonable day breakdown. Realistically, I think AI helps debug faster, and generate code faster. Possibly design work too, but I think this isn't really the case since AI workflows necessitate a lot  more  design work in order to make the AI generation deterministic. So looking at that day, if I was able to fully automate writing code  and  debugging issues so that it took 0 time at all (which I think is a very optimistic assessment of the actual speed ups AI provides), we're looking at a 2x speed up of an engineers productivity. If we think AI makes those things twice as fast (so 2 hours, instead of 4) the engineer is now at a 1.25x speed up. That's great, but it's hardly revolutionary. It'll change your output something like the way going from a team of 4 to a team of 5 might do. This is obviously complete conjecture and I'm sure the average time engineers spend on things is different, but I think there's an obvious take away. If you want to make claims about the performance impact of code, you need to know  where the code spends its time , and  what impact you're making on those sections of code . Similarly, if you want to know what performance gains are being made, you need to know  what engineers spend their time doing  and  what impact AI is having of those tasks . I've seen very little attempt to actually make realistic claims on that basis, and a lot of vibes-based "wooah, AI makes me so much faster" type claims. Those claims are obviously not nothing, but I wouldn't trust people's gut reactions to make serious claims about the overall productivity changes in our entire industry.

source_text:
Show HN: Atticus – Hold-to-talk voice assistant for macOS that runs on Claude -p
Hi HN! I'm Saarth. I'm in 9th grade, and I built Atticus. Atticus is a fast and cheap Mac assistant that can do tasks for you. You hold down Control-Option-Space, speak or type your task, be it complex or a simple browser search, and Atticus will get on it. The interesting part is that simple tasks, like opening apps, playing a Spotify playlist, or web queries, don't touch AI, and instead are processed locally and typically finish in under a second. For example, prompting Atticus to open apps takes around 0.08 seconds, sometimes even finishing before you finish your sentence, sort of like Jev. Any tasks that are more complicated will be sent to Claude via claude -p, meaning you never need an API key and Atticus will run on your existing Claude Pro or Max plan. By using this approach, costs are also cut down immensely, with, on average, tasks costing a fraction of a cent. To achieve Atticus' speed, it remembers shortcuts from each task it completes. When it does a task right for the first time, it saves its steps and replays them the next time without AI. For example, a workflow of creating a new meeting took about 30 seconds the first time around. Atticus then logs the exact steps to memory and takes 5-8 seconds on the next pass. To add to this, Atticus also learns about you as you use it more and from what's on your computer, including your name, your apps, and things you want it to remember, personalizing its answers to you. To combat the safety concerns over giving an AI unrestricted access to your device, Atticus has toggleable restrictions, so before anything is deleted, sent, bought, or written to a file, the user is prompted before that action. Some features I'm currently working on include a meeting copilot that capitalizes on Atticus' speed, allowing Atticus to listen in on meetings and answer questions in real time as they come in, personalized to the context of the meeting and what it knows about you. To run Atticus, macOS 26 or higher is required for its voice transcription features. The voice transcription is also done locally by macOS. Atticus is free, open source, and also very fresh, and I'm completely aware of its many rough edges, which is why I'd love to hear from everyone about what breaks and what you guys would like to see Atticus do!

source_text:
Human approval in n8n: what does the reviewer actually need to see?
Hello everyone, 
 I’m one of the creators of Ratifia, a play on “ratify.” We build 
human-in-the-loop tooling for approvals in automated workflows that are auditable and reliable. 
 The question I keep coming back to is whether the person receiving an approval 
request has enough to actually decide. Not whether the workflow paused 
correctly, but whether the human on the other end understood what they were 
being asked to approve and what would happen when they said yes. 
 The problem that led us here is that adding an approval step is usually 
straightforward. Making it work for the people involved is the hard part: 
getting the right context in front of the right person, handling the wait, and 
being able to say afterward what was approved and what actually happened. 
 Our existing design partners have shaped a lot of the product, and most of what 
they changed was on the human side of it: what the reviewer sees, how much 
context is too much, and what they need to know about where a value came from. 
Now I’d like to learn from different industries, different workflows, and 
different ideas about where the human belongs. 
 I know n8n has human review for tool calls, and for plenty of cases that is 
enough. Where we spend our time is the narrower question of keeping the action 
that runs tied to the approval that was given, and preserving the evidence 
you’ll need a month later. 
 Our view is that this isn’t purely a tooling problem. It takes good workflow 
patterns and software that makes those patterns practical. We want to develop 
both alongside people dealing with these problems in real projects. 
 That’s why I’m posting instead of building another feature. I’m looking for two 
or three people running production workflows with consequential or 
hard-to-reverse actions: refunds, customer emails, sensitive record changes, or 
money movement. 
 Being a design partner means we work directly with you on the integration rather 
than pointing you at docs. We start by recording which actions would have 
required approval, before anything blocks, so you see what it would do before 
you turn on enforcement. 
 In return, I’m looking for a real workflow and honest feedback, including “this 
is wrong.” We’ll learn the most from workflows where a mistaken action has a 
real consequence and someone is responsible for the outcome. 
 If that sounds like your setup, I’d like to hear what you’re building and where 
your current approach falls short. Reply here or DM me. You can also take a look 
at  ratifia.com . 
 P.S. 
The node lands on npm this week. Self-hosted, you install it from Settings, 
Community nodes. On Cloud you can run the same thing with HTTP Request nodes 
today.

title: MCP Server Trigger v2: tools/call right after session re-initialize succeeds but response is never delivered (hangs until 524)
raw_evidence_quote:
MCP Server Trigger v2: tools/call right after session re-initialize succeeds but response is never delivered (hangs until 524) 
<!-- Please follow the template below. Skip the questions that are not relevant to you. -->

Describe the problem/error/question

MCP Server Trigger (v2): a tools/call sent right after a session re-initialize runs successfully, but its response is never delivered, so the request hangs until Cloudflare returns 524.

When an MCP session expires, n8n answers the next tools/call
source_text:
MCP Server Trigger v2: tools/call right after session re-initialize succeeds but response is never delivered (hangs until 524) 
<!-- Please follow the template below. Skip the questions that are not relevant to you. -->

Describe the problem/error/question

MCP Server Trigger (v2): a tools/call sent right after a session re-initialize runs successfully, but its response is never delivered, so the request hangs until Cloudflare returns 524.

When an MCP session expires, n8n answers the next tools/call with 404 (session not found). The client (Claude Code, using @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, streamable HTTP) then sends initialize and notifications/initialized and immediately re-sends the same tools/call. n8n runs the tool and it succeeds in 2–5 s, but no response headers are ever written to that POST. The request hangs until n8n Cloud's Cloudflare front end returns 524. The execution stays open about 125 s and is recorded with status success at the moment the connection drops.

This happened on 9 of 17 session-expiry retries over five days (2026-10-05 to 2026-10-09). It never happened on any other tool call: 0 of the other 226 tool executions on the same workflow.

Request sequence (one representative case; all nine match):

t (UTC) | Request | Response -- | -- | -- 14:20:37.9 | POST tools/call (old session id) | 404 session not found 14:20:38.6 | POST initialize | 200, new mcp-session-id 14:20:39.0 | POST notifications/initialized | 202 14:20:39.2 | POST notifications/initialized (client sends it twice) | 202 ~14:20:39 | POST tools/call (same tool, new session id) | nothing until 14:22:44.6, then 524 14:20:41.4 | POST tools/list | 200 14:20:48.2 | POST tools/call (same tool, same new session, client sends it again) | 200 in ~2 s

Expected: a tools/call on a freshly initialized session returns its JSON-RPC result, as a JSON body or an SSE event on the POST, as soon as the tool finishes. That is what happens for every other call, including the client's own second attempt a few seconds later on the same session.

Actual: the tool runs and succeeds, but the result never reaches the POST that asked for it. The request gets no response headers at all, and the execution stays open until the connection is cut.

What we have not established: the hung call arrives within ~0.5 s of initialize, alongside the notifications/initialized posts and before tools/list. The 8 retries that succeeded were sent slightly later. A race between session setup and the first request on the new session would fit this (for example, the response being written to a transport other than the one the POST is waiting on), but we have not confirmed it.

Our workaround: the proxy in front of n8n now answers any POST that has no response headers after 30 s with a retryable error, so the client re-sends instead of waiting for the 524.

Reproduction outline (not yet tried in isolation):

  1. MCP Server Trigger v2 with any fast tool attached, published.

  2. Open a streamable-HTTP MCP session, then let it expire so the next tools/call gets 404.

  3. Immediately initialize a new session, send notifications/initialized, and without waiting for tools/list send the tools/call again.

  4. The tool node runs and succeeds in the execution log, but the POST never receives response headers.

What is the error message (if any)?

No n8n error. The execution is marked success. The client receives HTTP 524 from Cloudflare after ~100 s with no response headers from n8n.

Please share your workflow/screenshots/recording

The workflow is one MCP Server Trigger (@n8n/n8n-nodes-langchain.mcpTrigger, typeVersion 2, streamable HTTP, header authentication) with read-only tools attached: httpRequestTool (typeVersion 4.4) and built-in app tool nodes. Every tool returns in seconds. The workflow JSON contains internal endpoints, so we have not pasted it here. We can share it, with execution ids and exact timestamps, privately with the n8n team.

The client reaches the trigger through a stateless reverse proxy, one replica, that forwards mcp-session-id, mcp-protocol-version, content-type, accept and last-event-id unchanged, so requests arrive in the order the client sends them.

Share the output returned by the last node

For the hung call in the table above, the execution shows:

  • Tool node: startTime 14:20:39, executionTime 1,926 ms, executionStatus success, about 18 KB of output.

  • MCP Server Trigger node: run recorded at 14:22:44 (0 ms). The execution's startedAt/stoppedAt are 14:22:44.69 / 14:22:44.72, so it was recorded only when the connection closed, about 125 s after the tool finished.

Across all nine hung calls: tool runtime 1.9–5.0 s (all success), tool start to execution close 125 s every time, response size 7–64 KB. Every other tool execution in the period closed within ~2 s of its tool finishing; the slowest tool runtime of all 235 was 11.9 s.

Debug info

core

  • n8nVersion: 2.43.3 (the exact version at the time of each incident was not recorded)

  • platform: docker (cloud)

  • nodeJsVersion: 26.7.0

  • nodeEnv: production

  • database: sqlite

  • executionMode: regular

  • concurrency: 50

  • license: enterprise (sandbox)

storage

  • success: all

  • error: all

  • progress: false

  • manual: true

  • binaryMode: filesystem

pruning

  • enabled: true

  • maxAge: 720 hours

  • maxCount: 25000 executions

client

  • userAgent: mozilla/5.0 (macintosh; intel mac os x 10_15_7) applewebkit/537.36 (khtml, like gecko) chrome/155.0.0.0 safari/537.36

  • isTouchDevice: false

Ask HN: Fake abuse reports keep auto-blocking my site on Cloudflare
I run a small site on Cloudflare's Pro plan. Since 26 September, someone has filed the same fake abuse report against it six times. Each time, Cloudflare automatically puts a "Suspected Malware" warning on my homepage and login pages, and it stays until a person reviews it. The reports are word for word identical. They describe an "order" and product pages that have never existed on my site (they return 404). The file hash in the report doesn't match the hash in its own VirusTotal link, which returns "Item not found". Only the date changes, and twice it's been misspelled ("October 52026", "Octoboer 8 2026"). Cloudflare's team has cleared four of them. The reporter pastes the same text again within a day. The result is that my homepage has been blocked for most of two weeks, my traffic has halved, and Google is indexing the warning page instead of my site. I've opened support cases and requested reviews each time. I've had one reply, on 5 October, and nothing on a lasting fix. I'm not asking for special treatment. I'd like to know:
1. Is there a way to stop automatic mitigations from a reporter or text that has already been shown to be false?
2. Is there a manual-review setting for a domain?
3. Has anyone else seen the abuse form used like this, and how did it end? The same problem is described in my open case with Cloudflare (#02370521). Thanks for any pointers, and if anyone from Cloudflare's abuse team reads this, I'd welcome a reply.

source_text:
Show HN: Chkit – Schema, migrations and backfills for ClickHouse (like Drizzle)
Hey HN, im Marc, co-founder of ObsessionDB.
We are open sourcing ChKit, our tooling to manage schemas, migrations and backfills for clickhouse. I am a big fan of the type safety drizzle provides for the database. Manage the schema in typescript and generate migrations from it is a powerful workflow. I always wished something like it would exist for clickhouse, so we could manage our analytical workloads the same way. It didn't exist, so we build it. We build it after running ClickHouse at petabyte scale in our previous company, were we managed hundreds of tables, MVs and endpoints reading from them. The way it works: 1. You define your schema in typescript, with typed helpers for tables, mv, column types etc..
2. You generate the migration, that contains the DDL, to get your clickhouse instance from status quo to what your current typescript schema defines
3. Your CI can check for drift
4. You run the generated migration against production
5. You use the defined types in your code, to ingest your data while making sure it has the correct type.
   Bonus: if your schema change was BC breaking, we generate the sequence on how to backfill the data, into the intermediate table to migrate (this is quite the hard problem with large tables and schema evolution) In case you have already a clickhouse instance with a schema, you can pull it down and start using ChKit from where you are. Run our generator to setup the boilerplate:     npm create chkit@latest
  
If you folks are running clickhouse in production, I am curious to hear what other challenges you are running into.

source_text:
Microsoft Teams Trigger silently stops receiving messages after ~3 days (Graph subscription is never renewed)
### Bug Description

The **Microsoft Teams Trigger** (channel messages) creates a Microsoft Graph change-notification subscription when the workflow is published/activated, but nothing ever renews it. Graph caps `channelMessage` subscriptions at 4320 minutes (3 days), so the trigger stops receiving messages roughly 3 days after each activation or n8n restart. The workflow still shows as **Active**, no execution fails and no error is raised: the trigger is simply silent. In our case it went unnoticed for 12 days (messages with photos were not processed).

What we observed (delegated OAuth credential `microsoftTeamsOAuth2Api`; first seen on 2.39.10, same node code on 2.42.6):

1. After re-publishing the workflow, `GET /v1.0/subscriptions` listed one subscription for `/teams/{teamId}/channels/{channelId}/messages` with `expirationDateTime` exactly 72 h after creation (2026-10-09T17:13:25Z -> 2026-10-12T17:13:25Z). It was unchanged 3 days later, i.e. no renewal happened.
2. Graph lifecycle notifications (`@odata.type: "#microsoft.graph.subscription"`, only the subscription id present) are delivered to the workflow as normal trigger items shortly before expiry. Nothing handles them (no PATCH, no re-authorize, no re-create); users have to filter them out manually.
3. From reading `MicrosoftTeamsTrigger.node.ts`: `checkExists()` only lists subscriptions and keeps those valid for more than 5 minutes; `create()` creates them and `delete()` removes them. We could not find renewal logic or handling of `reauthorizationRequired` / `subscriptionRemoved`.

Related (not GitHub issues): https://community.n8n.io/t/problem-teams-trigger-webhook/147354 (users report the same ~3 day expiry; workarounds: nightly PATCH or nightly unpublish/publish).

### To Reproduce

1. Create a workflow with **Microsoft Teams Trigger** on a channel (resource: channel message) using a delegated OAuth credential.
2. Publish it and post a message in the channel: the workflow executes.
3. Wait more than 72 hours without republishing the workflow or restarting n8n.
4. Post a message in the channel: no execution is created. `GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/subscriptions` no longer lists a valid subscription for the channel.
5. Unpublish + publish again: it works for another ~3 days.

### Expected behavior

The trigger keeps working indefinitely while the workflow is active, as Microsoft requires apps to renew subscriptions before expiry (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/resources/subscription). Either renew the subscription periodically (`PATCH /subscriptions/{id}` with a new `expirationDateTime`, which also re-authorizes it), and/or handle the lifecycle notifications Graph sends (`reauthorizationRequired` -> PATCH; `subscriptionRemoved` -> re-create) instead of passing them to the workflow as items. At the very least, failing to keep the subscription alive should be visible (workflow status, execution error or log), since today the workflow looks healthy while it receives nothing.

Workaround we use: a separate scheduled workflow (twice a day) that does `GET /v1.0/subscriptions` with the same credential, picks the subscription whose `resource` matches the channel, and `PATCH`es its `expirationDateTime` to now + 4300 min; it alerts if none exists or the PATCH fails.

Show HN: Lemma, an IDE for reading mathematics (macOS, open source)
I built Lemma while working through The Elements of Statistical Learning (using the Preview app). Kept running into references like "(3.41)" or "by Theorem 2.3" forcing me to scroll back through the entire book. And whenever a proof wasn’t detailed enough, I'd screenshot it, ask ChatGPT to explain, then go back to the PDF to add manual notes. Got pretty annoying. That led me to Lemma: it reads a PDF once (locally), lets you jump around between equations, theorems, etc. without constantly scrolling. I gave it a VS Code look because yes, I'm addicted to VS Code (there are other themes for normal people). A non-exhaustive list of things it can do (right now): - References to theorems, equations, figures, citations and index entries are all clickable (you can peek at them without leaving the page) - You can ask an agent or ChatGPT Web for explanations, longer proofs with one click, save the output in Lemma - When the pdf says “it is easy to show” or “proof left to the reader”, you can write the missing steps in LaTeX, and Lemma checks it on random numerical inputs and gives counterexamples if it’s wrong. You can also fold proofs to try them yourself first, and keep notes attached to specific passages (with exports to Markdown, Anki and Jupyter). Built in Swift/SwiftUI using PDFKit. The analysis runs in a helper process at low priority. No account, no telemetry, and it's GPL.
It’s for macOS 15+ only for now (unless a lot of people find it useful, then I’ll probably do it for other OSes).
It still struggles with some PDFs (scanned ones, other languages, different numbering, etc.) If you try it on whatever you're reading and encounter some problems, feel free to open an issue!

source_text:
Show HN: Singularity – memory that makes coding agents cheaper on repeat work
Coding agents start every session from zero. Ask Claude Code for a change like one it made last week and it reads the same files again, falls into the same test traps again, and you pay for all of it again. Singularity learns from your finished sessions (change committed, tests passing): where each kind of change goes in this repo, how it gets checked, and the mistakes made along the way. When the next task starts, a hook hands the agent the workflows that fit, pointed at the code as it is today. Picking them is plain text matching with no model call. It stores where to edit, never the code itself. Results, medians of 3–4 runs per side, hidden tests decide pass/fail, every run passed. On excalidraw: - A long task with four changes, all of kinds memory had learned: 1.9M → 423k tokens, $0.81 → $0.30, 28.5 → 9.5 turns. - The same kind of task, but two of the four changes were bugs it had never seen: 39% fewer tokens, 38% lower cost. The unseen bugs cost the same with or without memory. - Where it doesn't help: small tasks in validator.js and one-off bug fixes. The difference there is about zero, within noise. Each measurement was written down before it was run. The plans and results are in the repo. Caveats: 3–4 runs per side, mostly one repo. Only Claude Code sessions are learned from; Codex, Gemini CLI and Droid get the hand-over through their hooks. Learning uses your Claude account (about $0.25 a round, capped at $1 a day, and only if you opt in). Everything is stored locally in ~/.singularity. Install (Windows PowerShell and more options in the README):     curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pandacover/singularity/main/install.sh | sh
  
I'd love to hear where it breaks on your repos, and what memory should carry for one-off work like bug fixes.

### Bug Description

The AI Assistant repeatedly failed to save changes to an existing workflow, despite successful TypeScript SDK validation.

The captured build-workflow calls included both a valid filePath and sourceCode: "". After a failed build, the referenced source file was confirmed to be 0 bytes.

The build returned:

Default export is not a workflow. Make sure your file has: export default workflow(...)

The Assistant retried the same approach multiple times, including after stating that it would omit sourceCode. The requested changes were never saved.

Impact
The requested scheduling and lookback changes were not saved. The existing live workflow remained unchanged, and no workflow execution was attempted.

### To Reproduce

Observed sequence:

Ask the AI Assistant to modify an existing workflow.
The Assistant exports it to a .workflow.ts workspace file and applies scoped edits.
SDK validation succeeds with “no issues found”.
The Assistant calls build-workflow with the file path and an empty sourceCode string.
The build fails with the error above.
Inspecting the workspace file shows that it is now 0 bytes.
The Assistant re-exports, edits, validates, and retries, but encounters the same failure.


### Expected behavior

When building from filePath, the Assistant should omit sourceCode and preserve the existing source file.

If an empty sourceCode value is supplied, the tool should reject it without overwriting the file, or otherwise handle it safely. After repeated identical failures, the Assistant should stop rather than repeat the same save approach.

- [ ] Search plan używa nazw problemów, workaroundów i opisów frustracji w językach właściwych dla rynku/source markets; nie tylko 'winning products'.

source_text:
Show HN: Delegator – Stop juggling coding-agent sessions
I wanted to share Delegator with the HN community.  delegator gives you a personal inbox to manage your tasks that is completely local to your machine. Backstory: Like everyone else, I've been experimenting with different AI-assisted development workflows.  I realized I was having difficulty with all the context switching between tasks.  Asking agents to develop code ends up taking about 5-10 minutes usually for well-scoped tasks.  At the beginning I would read the AI output as it went along and sometimes interrupt to guide it.  But as LLMs have gotten better, there's less need to do that.  So I would spin up another task during the latency and then another.  (I wrote a little bit about this previously here  https://mattmccormick.ca/we-re-all-managers-now-my-journey-i...  ) Jumping back and forth between terminals with the Agent being at different stages was mentally taxing.  I experimented with some different options and ended up realizing that to avoid the drain of context-switching, what I really needed was a queue. Delegator works by putting all scoped tasks through the system.  It stops when the ready queue has reached your configured limit.  This is to prevent too much work from piling up waiting for review.  It also presents the work from getting too far ahead in case any issues are found as part of development. I also realized that for most tasks, agents can be treated as a background process.  You pass in the work to the process.  It processes it and then gives you an output to review.  All changes are made in git worktrees for safety. Who's it for?  Delegator is for engineers who still want to understand the code and changes.  It's not for vibe-coding or exploratory work.  Don't get me wrong, I'll still spin up an agent session for brainstorming design options.  But once I'm aligned on a direction, I'll then ask the agent to break down the work into "dg tickets".  Since Delegator is a local program, agents can interact with it quickly and seamlessly. Right now it's just CLI based but I'm looking to expand this into a GUI/Desktop App so I would be interested in any feedback you have.  Let me know if you have any questions and I'll respond.  The code is source available so you can check it out at  https://github.com/alcubie/delegator  if you want to check anything.
buyer_activity_quote: Your other comment is flagged as dead so I'll reply here: > I like the idea of using a “local inbox for agent sessions” because switching between different contexts can be more frustrating than the actual time it takes the agent to run. > But I’m curious about how you see the inbox being useful beyond simply storing and replaying conversations. > A few things would help me understand the practical value: > What does a session actually contain? Is it just the conversation, or does it also include things like prompts, code changes, test results, Git commits, and other context? Can you reliably replay a session? Ideally, someone should be able to see what task was given, what the agent changed, what tests were run, and whether the task actually passed. What happens when work gets interrupted? If I pause one task and start another, can I come back later without losing the context or putting the project into a confusing state? How do you prove the work was completed? For example, can the system show the tests that were run, the changes made, and whether they passed? How is everything kept safe? If everything runs locally, that's great, but I'd still want to know how filesystem, network access, and logs are controlled. > Even a small example showing something like how long it takes to go from starting a task to getting a working result, compared with the current workflow, would make the benefits much easier to understand. --- Thanks for the questions!  I like your suggestion about providing a small example.  I'll put that together.  Email me at matt@alcubi.ai and I will send it to you when it's ready.  In the meantime, this page from the documentation may help to provide some of the details you're looking for  https://alcubi.ai/delegator/docs/dev/concepts/ticket-lifecyc...  A session includes the scoped task request (ticket) and the code changes that are made on a separate git branch in a new worktree.  You can enter the agent session at anytime with the "dg chat" command.  That will allow you to look into the details of how the agent accomplished its work.  So even though the runs execute in the background, the agent session is always available if you want to jump into it.  I'll use this command when something was unclear to ask for follow-up changes.  The agent will still have all the context in its session from the work it previously did so there's no extra context loading needed in these case. If works gets interrupted, the ticket status moves to the Failed inbox.  You'll see that clearly from the output of the "dg" command which shows the various inboxes.  When this happens I'll use "dg chat" to attach to the agent session to understand what went wrong.  Usually, this is something like the Claude/Codex API being down.  When the API is back up, I run "dg restart" to restart the processing from where it left off.  Since all work is done in separate branches and worktrees there's no ability for your project's main branch to be left in a confusing state. The agents will run your test suite that's setup.  delegator is just the orchestration layer.  You can customize any steps you'd like the agents to follow via your AGENTS.md file.  That will be taken into account when the agents run.  So for example, you could add in your AGENTS.md file that for any delegator ticket they work on to include details in the commit of tests that were run.  It's very flexible like that so you can customize it for your setup. For safety, I've gotten to the point where I trust that agents are only accessing data that they need so there are currently no guardrails in place.  This is something you could add to your AGENTS.md file to get information about but that's not deterministic.  I could add in features to support this.  Please email me at my email above to let me know a bit more about what you'd like to see and I can work on that. Hope this helps and thanks for taking a look!

📰 Weekly Digest — 2026-W42 (October 05 – October 12, 2026)
# Weekly Digest — 2026-W42

*October 05 – October 12, 2026*

# Weekly Digest: October 05 – October 12, 2026

## Executive summary

This week was dominated by AI platform and agent engineering updates across GitHub and Azure, with major momentum around Copilot controls, local sandboxing, agent governance, evaluation, and new model availability in Microsoft Foundry. Developer tooling also saw meaningful operational changes, especially around Azure CLI/PowerShell authentication and API compatibility, plus new Azure Functions agent capabilities and continued investment in Aspire and VS Code. On the platform side, Azure highlighted Kubernetes, Arc, API Management, and integration scenarios, while Azure Updates carried an unusually heavy retirement signal that teams should review closely. Security and infrastructure coverage reinforced two strategic themes: prepare now for post-quantum and AI-era risk, and modernize observability, networking, and cluster operations before forced transitions arrive.

## GitHub

GitHub’s updates centered on Copilot governance, model rollout, developer experience improvements, and platform-scale security. The biggest themes were tighter enterprise controls, better accessibility and workflow ergonomics, and continued investment in secret detection and agent-scale development infrastructure.

- Copilot for JetBrains added new controls and chat improvements.
- GitHub Copilot weekly releases for October 5 bundled the latest product changes.
- CodeQL 2.27.2 improved analysis for C++, Go, Rust, and JavaScript.
- Copilot code review gained new organization billing options and controls.
- Claude Haiku 5.5 became available in GitHub Copilot.
- Local sandboxing for GitHub Copilot reached general availability.
- GitHub introduced a purpose-built model for leaked secret detection.
- GitHub emphasized that secret protection must scale with software.
- Triage role users or higher can now archive pull requests.
- Draft pull requests now count toward pull request limits.

## Data & AI

Azure’s Data & AI news was heavily focused on building, evaluating, governing, and optimizing AI agents in Microsoft Foundry. Alongside new models and retrieval patterns, several posts tackled practical concerns such as evaluation quality, cost efficiency, governance, analytics integration, and database connectivity performance.

- Microsoft-Decision-1 was introduced in Microsoft Foundry for decision and classification workloads.
- Claude Haiku 5.5 is now available in Microsoft Foundry.
- Grok 4.7 was introduced on Microsoft Foundry.
- Microsoft published guidance on closing the AI agent governance gap with Microsoft Foundry.
- Foundry posts explored evaluating voice agents, including Voice User Simulator and multi-turn evaluator reliability.
- Foundry IQ guidance covered metadata-aware agentic RAG when answers are not directly in documents.
- Microsoft shared techniques for making evaluations more cost-efficient.
- A practical guide covered Azure Document Intelligence and Azure Content Understanding.
- Guidance outlined building production agents in three stages rather than one.
- SqlClient’s new connection pool was introduced for faster parallel connections.

## Developer Tools

Developer tooling updates combined IDE releases, authentication and compatibility changes, new agent-development guidance, and Azure Functions enhancements. The most urgent items are around Azure CLI/Azure PowerShell readiness for Key Vault and Azure AD Graph retirement, while the most forward-looking items focus on agentic development and cloud-native app tooling.

- Visual Studio Code 1.141 and 1.142 Insiders were released.
- Azure Key Vault control plane API changes require upgrades for Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell users.
- Azure AD Graph API retirement requires action for older Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell versions.
- Azure CLI on macOS received a security upgrade with native broker authentication.
- Azure Functions introduced Agent bindings for Python function apps in preview.
- Azure Functions also added managed connectors to connect to more services.
- Hosted Skills in Azure Functions gained dynamic workflows for durable, AI-led event-driven apps.
- Microsoft introduced the Agent Experience practitioner playbook and an explainer on AX.
- Aspire updates added dashboard persistence and brought Native AOT to the dashboard.
- .NET shipped a faster, lighter C# Dev Kit and guidance for UI testing in UWP and WinUI 3 with MSTest.

## Azure Platform

Azure platform announcements focused on application modernization, managed services, governance for AI integrations, and Kubernetes and GitOps operations. The standout items were Anyscale on Azure reaching GA, Arc and AKS management improvements, and growing API Management relevance for MCP and agent governance scenarios.

- Anyscale on Azure is now generally available.
- GitOps with the Argo CD extension for AKS is now generally available.
- Kubernetes clusters can now be onboarded to Azure Arc with the Multicloud Connector in public preview.
- Microsoft Agent 365 and Azure API Management integration was highlighted for MCP governance.
- Logic Apps Automation announced free grant and pricing updates.
- Azure Managed Redis deployment automation was introduced.
- Azure Storage Actions can bulk change blob tiers.
- API Management service tag network rules were updated.
- Azure Integration Services showcased a governed, event-driven AI intake pipeline.
- Azure published a cost-focused look at running Qwen3.8-27B on a $2 H100 Azure Spot VM.

## Azure Infrastructure

Infrastructure coverage was smaller in volume but important for platform engineers operating secure and connected estates. Networking, Key Vault operational lessons, and AKS host-level capability expansion were the main themes.

- AKS multi-NIC support powered by DRANET entered public preview.
- Azure published lessons learned for Key Vault and BYOK deployments.
- Azure VPN Gateway guidance showed how to proactively monitor tunnel disconnections.
- Microsoft highlighted its presence and priorities at OCP Global Summit 2026.

## Containers & Kubernetes

This week’s Kubernetes items were both operationally significant, focusing on lower-level runtime and node behavior changes that can directly affect workload stability and performance. Platform teams should pay attention to cgroup v2 migration implications and the emerging use of node swap.

- Kubernetes published guidance on the shift to cgroup v2 and what teams need to know.
- Kubernetes also covered scaling workloads with node swap.

## Security

Security coverage emphasized readiness for next-generation threats, especially post-quantum transitions and AI-driven vulnerability management. The guidance was strategic but directly relevant to architects planning identity, detection, and risk programs.

- Microsoft urged organizations to start testing certificate ecosystems for post-quantum authentication.
- Microsoft Sentinel introduced the ASIM EmailEvent schema.
- Microsoft shared three lessons from frontier AI vulnerability research.
- CISO perspectives focused on managing vulnerability risks in the age of AI.

## Governance & Operations

Governance coverage was limited this week but useful for teams using deployment analysis to reduce operational friction. The focus was on improving the signal-to-noise ratio in change review workflows.

- Azure Governance detailed noise reduction improvements in Stacks What-If.

## Azure Updates

Azure Updates was heavily weighted toward lifecycle notices, with multiple retirements that could affect platform, data, Java, App Service, Arc, and AKS users. At the same time, several GA and preview launches expanded AKS networking, WAF controls, backup, HorizonDB, and Marketplace and SQL capabilities.

- Retirement: Azure Deployment Environments will be retired on February 22, 2027.
- Retirement: Microsoft Dev Box will be retired on September 18, 2028.
- Retirement: Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc enabled Kubernetes clusters.
- Retirement: Azure App Service on Azure Stack Hub.
- Retirement: support for Java 8, 11, and 17 will end on September 1, 2027.
- Generally available: Managed StandardV2 NAT Gateway for AKS.
- Generally available: WAF exceptions for Azure Application Gateway and Azure Front Door.
- Public preview: Microsoft Agent 365 integration with Azure API Management.
- Public preview: Azure Backup for PostgreSQL flexible server and elastic cluster (v2).
- Public preview: IPv6 support for Application Gateway WAF.

## Ecosystem

The broader ecosystem mix this week included infrastructure-as-code, community DevOps experimentation, and Oracle partnership visibility. While lighter than Azure and GitHub news, these items may still be useful to practitioners watching adjacent toolchains and partner ecosystems.

- Terraform released v1.17.0-rc1.
- A DevOps community post explored using Whisper, FFMPEG, and yt-dlp to analyze sermons for red flags.
- Microsoft promoted its presence at Oracle AI World 2026.

source_text:
Instance-level MCP: `search_workflow_executions` always fails output-schema validation after upgrading to 2.42.6
### Bug Description

After upgrading a self-hosted instance from 2.39.8 to 2.42.6, the instance-level MCP tool `search_workflow_executions` fails on every call from Claude (claude.ai custom connector) with:

```
Structured content does not match the tool's output schema: data must NOT have additional properties
```

It fails even with a filter that returns zero executions (a workflow with no executions), so the extra property seems to be on the root object of the structured response, not on individual execution rows. Other read tools work on the same connection: `search_workflows`, `get_workflow_details`, `get_workflow_execution` (metadata only), `search_nodes`, `get_node_types`. Refreshing the client's tool list does not help (same 13 tools, same schema). The same call worked on 2.39.8 with the same client and scopes (`workflow:read` + `execution:read`).

**Additional context**
Probably related to a change in the response shape (pagination or count fields) that was not reflected in the tool's `outputSchema` with `additionalProperties: false`. Clients that don't validate structured content may not notice.

### To Reproduce

1. Self-hosted n8n 2.42.6 (Docker, Postgres, `n8nio/runners` external), Instance-level MCP enabled, OAuth client with `workflow:read` + `execution:read`.
2. From an MCP client that validates `structuredContent` against `outputSchema` (Claude), call `search_workflow_executions` with any arguments, e.g. `{ "workflowId": "<any exposed workflow>", "limit": 5 }`.
3. The client rejects the result with the error above.

### Expected behavior

The tool's `structuredContent` matches its declared `outputSchema` (or the schema declares the new property), as in 2.39.8.

### Debug Info

- n8n version: 2.42.6 (self-hosted, Docker), upgraded from 2.39.8
- Database: Postgres 16
- Execution mode: regular (main) + external task runners
- MCP client: Claude (claude.ai custom connector), OAuth
- Hosting: Coolify

### Operating System

Ubuntu Linux 24.04 (Docker, Coolify)

### n8n Version

2.42.6

### Node.js Version

v26.7.0

### Database

PostgreSQL

### Execution mode

main (default)

### Hosting

self hosted

Argan Oil Market Summary: Key Trends, Growth Drivers, Applications, and Future Opportunities
Understanding the Argan Oil Market

Argan oil has evolved from a traditional Moroccan ingredient into a valuable raw material for cosmetics, personal care, wellness, and selected food applications. Extracted from the kernels of the argan tree (Argania spinosa), the oil is recognized for its fatty acid composition, tocopherols, and other naturally occurring compounds. Its distinctive properties have helped establish demand among consumers seeking plant-derived ingredients for skin nourishment, hair conditioning, and premium beauty formulations.

The [argan oil market summary](https://www.pristinemarketinsights.com/argan-oil-market-report) highlights an industry shaped by changing consumer preferences, expanding beauty and personal care applications, sustainability concerns, and the need for reliable sourcing. Although the market benefits from interest in natural ingredients, its development depends on more than consumer enthusiasm. Limited agricultural supply, variations in oil quality, processing costs, and the importance of product authenticity all influence commercial performance.

As brands increasingly emphasize ingredient transparency and responsible sourcing, argan oil occupies a distinctive position between traditional agricultural production and modern specialty ingredient manufacturing.

Key Factors Driving Market Growth

Increasing Demand for Natural Beauty Ingredients

The shift toward plant-based ingredients continues to influence product development across skincare, haircare, and body care. Consumers are paying closer attention to ingredient lists and seeking products that support moisturizing, conditioning, and everyday skin and hair maintenance.

Argan oil fits these preferences because it can be incorporated into facial oils, moisturizers, shampoos, conditioners, hair masks, body lotions, and leave-in treatments. Its relatively versatile formulation profile allows manufacturers to use it as a primary ingredient in premium products or as one component in blended formulations.

However, natural positioning alone does not guarantee commercial success. Brands must demonstrate product suitability, maintain consistent quality, and communicate realistic benefits without making unsupported therapeutic claims.

Expansion of Premium Haircare and Skincare

Premium beauty products represent an important application area. Haircare manufacturers use argan oil in formulations designed to improve manageability, reduce the appearance of dryness, and enhance shine. In skincare, formulators incorporate it into products intended to soften and condition the skin.

The ingredient also supports product differentiation. Companies can develop lightweight facial oils, intensive hair treatments, overnight conditioning products, and multipurpose beauty oils for consumers who prefer streamlined personal care routines.

Growth opportunities are particularly relevant to brands that combine effective formulation, convenient packaging, clear ingredient information, and competitive pricing. At the same time, products must meet consumer expectations for texture, absorption, fragrance, and performance.

Major Applications Across Industries

Cosmetics and Personal Care

Cosmetics and personal care constitute a central application category for argan oil. Its presence in moisturizers, serums, cleansers, hair oils, and styling products allows manufacturers to address different consumer needs using a recognizable botanical ingredient.

The premium segment often places greater emphasis on traceability, packaging, formulation quality, and brand positioning. Meanwhile, mass-market manufacturers may focus on affordability, product accessibility, and the inclusion of argan oil within broader ingredient blends.

For suppliers, these differences create opportunities to serve multiple customer groups. Nevertheless, commercial buyers generally require reliable specifications, stable supply arrangements, and appropriate documentation before integrating an ingredient into large-scale production.

Food and Culinary Applications

Food-grade argan oil serves a separate market from cosmetic-grade oil. Traditionally used in Moroccan cuisine, culinary argan oil is valued for its distinctive nutty flavor and its role in regional food preparation. It may be used in dressings, dips, and selected finished foods.

This segment depends on careful processing, suitable storage, and protection against oxidation. Roasting practices, extraction methods, and handling conditions can influence the oil's sensory characteristics and quality.

Manufacturers must also distinguish culinary products from cosmetic formulations through appropriate processing controls, labeling, and food safety procedures. Maintaining this separation is essential because the intended use determines the relevant quality requirements.

Regional Production and Market Opportunities

Morocco's Central Role in Supply

Morocco remains the principal origin of commercial argan oil because the argan tree is closely associated with the country's ecological landscape and traditional production systems. The geographic concentration of raw materials creates a strong connection between international demand and conditions in local producing communities.

Argan oil production can provide income opportunities for rural households and processing cooperatives. In particular, women-led cooperatives have played an important role in traditional kernel processing, product preparation, and the development of community-based enterprises.

However, supply expansion is constrained by the biological characteristics of the argan tree, environmental pressures, and the time required to establish productive trees. Climate variability, water stress, land degradation, and changing agricultural conditions can affect the long-term availability of raw materials.

International Demand and Distribution

Demand extends beyond Morocco through cosmetic manufacturers, specialty ingredient distributors, premium retailers, online stores, and international beauty brands. Markets with established personal care industries provide opportunities for suppliers that can demonstrate consistent quality and dependable delivery.

E-commerce has also improved access to niche botanical oils. Smaller brands can reach consumers directly, explain sourcing practices, and introduce specialized formulations without relying exclusively on conventional retail distribution.

Nevertheless, international expansion requires attention to import regulations, product labeling, packaging standards, and customer expectations. Suppliers that adapt their documentation and distribution strategies to individual markets may be better positioned to build durable commercial relationships.

Challenges Affecting Market Development

Supply Limitations and Price Volatility

Argan oil production involves labor-intensive harvesting and kernel extraction. These activities can increase production costs, particularly when manufacturers require carefully selected kernels, controlled processing, and detailed quality verification.

Limited raw material availability can also make supply less responsive to sudden increases in demand. When brands expand product lines or compete for premium-grade ingredients, suppliers may face pressure to maintain consistent volumes without compromising quality.

Long-term sourcing agreements, improved processing efficiency, and stronger relationships with producer cooperatives can help reduce operational uncertainty. However, these measures cannot completely eliminate environmental and agricultural risks.

Authenticity, Adulteration, and Quality Control

Product authenticity is another significant concern. Differences in grade, extraction method, storage conditions, and ingredient composition can affect the characteristics of commercial oils. Mislabeling or blending with lower-cost oils can undermine consumer confidence and create regulatory problems.

Businesses can address these concerns through supplier qualification, batch-level documentation, appropriate analytical testing, and traceability systems. Clear specifications should identify the intended application, relevant quality parameters, and acceptable handling conditions.

For premium brands, transparent sourcing information can also strengthen customer trust. Credible claims supported by documented practices are more valuable than broad statements about purity or sustainability that cannot be verified.

Emerging Trends and Strategic Opportunities

Traceability and Responsible Sourcing

Responsible sourcing is becoming increasingly important as companies examine the environmental and social implications of botanical ingredients. In the argan oil sector, this includes protecting the natural ecosystem, supporting producer livelihoods, and encouraging practices that maintain long-term resource availability.

Businesses may explore direct purchasing relationships, transparent payment structures, cooperative partnerships, and improved tracking from raw material collection to finished product manufacturing. Such measures can help improve accountability throughout the supply chain.

Sustainability claims should remain specific and evidence-based. Environmental benefits depend on actual production practices, land management, resource use, and supply chain conditions rather than on the ingredient's natural origin alone.

Product Innovation and Value-Added Formulations

Another opportunity lies in moving beyond conventional standalone oils. Manufacturers can incorporate argan oil into targeted haircare systems, multipurpose skincare products, scalp treatments, and formulations designed for particular textures or application preferences.

Innovation may also focus on packaging that limits exposure to air and light, convenient dispensing systems, and formats suited to travel or daily use. For suppliers, offering consistent technical information and application guidance can improve their attractiveness to formulation teams.

There is also scope for developing distinct product lines for different price points. Carefully formulated blended products can improve accessibility, while premium offerings may emphasize verified sourcing, specialized processing, and detailed ingredient provenance.

Future Outlook

The future development of the argan oil industry will depend on the balance between consumer demand, agricultural resilience, product quality, and responsible commercial practices. Interest in natural beauty ingredients provides a favorable foundation, but competition from other botanical oils means that argan oil suppliers must continue to demonstrate practical value.

Companies that invest in traceability, dependable supplier relationships, appropriate quality testing, and application-specific product development may be better equipped to navigate changing market conditions. Protecting the ecological systems that support argan production will also remain essential to maintaining long-term supply.

Ultimately, the strongest opportunities are likely to emerge where traditional production knowledge meets modern formulation expertise and transparent business practices. Rather than relying solely on the popularity of natural ingredients, industry participants can build lasting demand by delivering consistent products, supporting responsible sourcing, and responding to clearly defined customer needs.

> Im not labelling any job stupid, im simply saying they are simple and there is no justification to pay hundreds of dollars a week for anything that 
> Im not labelling any job stupid, im simply saying they are simple and there is no justification to pay hundreds of dollars a week for anything that AI may help. Neither was I; I was saying that the US spending 9% of its own GDP looks a bit silly if that AI is only used within the USA's own economy. > No argument about calculators, but most job wouldnt pay hundreds of dollars a week for the utility of a calculator. Today vs. before the tech existed? Today: That's because calculators cost single-digit dollars/pounds/euros. Yet if you took a calculator back in time a century, it's not inconceivable that businesses  whose job involves lots of arithmetic  would value it at 10-15% of average wages, given the labour it would save. However, as you may have noticed, a calculator doesn't do every job. I see the same applying to AI, at least for now: for jobs where it's useful, it's worth 10-15% of wages. This isn't all jobs. Regardless of if it was all jobs or not, the tech gets cheaper, and just as nobody can charge more than a single digit $£€ for a basic 4-function calculator, nobody will be able to charge 10-15% of average wages for 2026 AI even a year from now let alone a century. > Your friend might be good with their hands, but they are not going to have the equipment for most jobs. WHen you buy the services of a plumber or any other tradesperson you are not only buying their skills, you are also leveraging their equipment. I don't mean "your friend". I mean pretend you're founding a new house repair firm: do you hire expert plumbers, or do you hire (presumably in a few years because neither the AI nor the AR is good enough today) random people willing to follow instructions from their AR glasses? You've bought all the equipment etc. the same in both cases. Who do you hire? And when everyone does that, do you as a customer prefer to hire the cheap company whose staff are as described, or the traditional firm that's 3x the price? Before you scoff:  this kind of thing has happened repeatedly with previous technologies . The main difference with the current architecture of modern AI is how general purpose it is, not that this is new. Previous architectures of AI were more like a normal technology, making one thing obsolete at a time, like  manually reading letters in a post sorting office , but just that and nothing else. High-skill roles get some automation, that turns them into low-skill roles. Suddenly, their bosses don't need to spend so much on wages to get the tasks done.  That's  the point with my cashier example. Someone working as a cashier in 1876 needed to be good at mental arithmetic, if I showed them a pocket calculator they might be impressed but in this context I'd expect them to be insulted: why would they need that for their job? Then the mechanical one was invented (to avoid embezzlement), and suddenly their bosses didn't need to hire people with that skill.
